# Purpose

`simulate_joinme_mix()` generates data from the finite latent-progress model
fitted by `joinme_mix()`. Its purpose is not merely to produce visibly
separated trajectories. It provides a controlled experiment in which the
class-generating distribution, allocation probabilities, longitudinal
measurement model, covariance regression, event process and censoring
mechanism are all known.

This makes the simulator suitable for:

1. parameter-recovery studies;
2. assessment of posterior class probabilities;
3. comparison of candidate class counts;
4. investigation of weak separation and rare classes;
5. evaluation of survival associations under latent heterogeneity; and
6. calibration of plots and predictive summaries against known truth.

The simulator uses the ordinary `simulate_joinme()` engine. The sole
statistical alteration is the distribution of selected standardised
random-effect coordinates. Consequently, marker-specific response families,
distributional regressions, irregular observation schedules, left truncation,
censoring, association transformations and baseline hazards have the same
meaning in ordinary and mixture simulation.

# Longitudinal model

For subject \(i=1,\ldots,n\), marker \(d=1,\ldots,D\), and time \(t\), let

\[
\eta_{id}(t)
=
\boldsymbol{x}_{id}(t)^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}
+
\boldsymbol{z}_{i}(t)^\top\boldsymbol{u}_i
+
\boldsymbol{z}_{d}(t)^\top\boldsymbol{v}_d
+
\boldsymbol{z}_{id}(t)^\top\boldsymbol{w}_{id}.
\]

Here:

- \(\boldsymbol{u}_i\) is the subject random-effect block;
- \(\boldsymbol{v}_d\) is the marker random-effect block; and
- \(\boldsymbol{w}_{id}\) is the nested subject-by-marker block.

The observation distribution is marker-specific:

\[
Y_{id}(t)\mid\eta_{id}(t),\boldsymbol{\psi}_{id}(t)
\sim
\mathcal{F}_d\left[
g_d^{-1}\{\eta_{id}(t)\},
\boldsymbol{\psi}_{id}(t)
\right],
\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\psi}_{id}(t)\) may contain scale, degrees of freedom,
dispersion, skewness, sample-size or quantile parameters generated through
`formulaDist`.

# Standardised latent representation

The subject and marker effects are constructed from standardised latent
vectors:

\[
\boldsymbol{u}_i=L_u\boldsymbol{z}_{u,i},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{v}_d=L_v\boldsymbol{z}_{v,d}.
\]

The subject-specific covariance factor for the nested block is

\[
L_i=L_i\{\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathrm{cov},i},\boldsymbol{z}_{L,i}\},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{w}_{id}
=
\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{r}_{w})L_i\boldsymbol{z}_{w,id}.
\]

The latent-progress mixture is defined on selected coordinates of
\(\boldsymbol{z}_{u,i}\), \(\boldsymbol{z}_{v,d}\),
\(\boldsymbol{z}_{L,i}\), and the standardised marker-weight perturbations.
It is not defined directly on the covariance-scaled realised effects.
Simulation at the standardised level is essential: it preserves the
interpretation of component locations when the ordinary random-effect
standard deviations or correlation matrices change.

# Component model

Let \(G=\texttt{n_clusters}\), and let \(C_j\) denote the latent class for an
allocation unit \(j\). For packed mixture coordinate \(r=1,\ldots,K\),

\[
Z_{jr}\mid C_j=g
\sim
D\left(\mu_{gr},s_{gr}\right),
\qquad
g=1,\ldots,G.
\]

The family \(D\) follows `shrinkage`:

\[
D =
\begin{cases}
t_6, & \texttt{shrinkage}=0,\\
\mathrm{Laplace}, & \texttt{shrinkage}=1,\\
\mathrm{Normal}, & \texttt{shrinkage}=2.
\end{cases}
\]

Coordinates are conditionally independent inside a component. Dependence is
induced through the common allocation \(C_j\), and the ordinary covariance
factor is subsequently applied to the subject or marker block.

Unselected subject, marker and covariance-regression coordinates remain
standard Normal.

# Natural allocation domains

There are two natural allocation domains.

## Subject domain

The types `"subject"`, `"corr"` and `"vcov"` use one class \(C_i^{(I)}\) per
subject. If compatible types are selected, the same label governs the selected
coordinates of \(\boldsymbol{z}_{u,i}\) and
\(\boldsymbol{z}_{L,i}\):

\[
p\left(
\boldsymbol{z}_{u,i}^{*},
\boldsymbol{z}_{L,i}^{*}
\right)
=
\sum_{g=1}^{G}
\pi_{ig}^{(I)}
p_g(\boldsymbol{z}_{u,i}^{*})
p_g(\boldsymbol{z}_{L,i}^{*}).
\]

## Marker domain

The type `"marker"` uses one class \(C_d^{(M)}\) per marker:

\[
p\left(
\boldsymbol{z}_{v,d}^{*}
\right)
=
\sum_{g=1}^{G}
\pi_{dg}^{(M)}
p_g(\boldsymbol{z}_{v,d}^{*}).
\]

Combining types therefore does not create \(G^2\) classes. The simulator and
fitted model both retain exactly \(G\).

# Class-probability regression

At zero covariates, the class probabilities are
\(\boldsymbol{\pi}=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_G)\). For allocation unit \(j\),

\[
\Pr(C_j=g\mid\boldsymbol{x}_j)
=
\frac{
\exp\{\log(\pi_g)+\boldsymbol{x}_{jg}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}_g\}
}{
\sum_{h=1}^{G}
\exp\{\log(\pi_h)+\boldsymbol{x}_{jh}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}_h\}
}.
\]

`formulaCluster` constructs the design vectors. A shared formula uses the same
formulaic structure for every non-reference class. A list of `n_clusters`
formulae permits a different predictor for each class. A named list separates
the subject and marker domains.

The formula intercept is removed. Baseline class frequencies belong in
`class_parameters$probability`; covariate effects belong in
`class_parameters$coefficient`.

# Label identification

Mixture likelihoods are invariant to permutation of class labels unless an
identification convention is imposed.

- `cluster_ordering = "intercept"` requires strict ordering of the selected
  random-intercept component locations. Only that coordinate is constrained;
  slope and other locations remain unrestricted.
- `cluster_ordering = "probability"` requires strictly increasing baseline
  probabilities.
- `cluster_ordering = "none"` imposes no ordering.

For class-specific formula lists, the default is `"none"`. Otherwise the
default is `"intercept"`, matching `joinme_mix()`.

In simulation the allocations are explicitly sampled, so label switching is
not a computational problem. The ordering is nevertheless enforced in the
generative parameters so that truth and posterior summaries use comparable
labels.

# Event process

When a survival process is present, the hazard retains the ordinary JoiNMe
form:

\[
h_i(t)
=
h_0(t)
\exp\left[
\boldsymbol{w}_i(t)^\top\boldsymbol{\gamma}
+
\mathcal{A}_i(t)
\right].
\]

The association predictor \(\mathcal{A}_i(t)\) may use current value, current
slope, marker-specific value or slope, covariance, or correlation features.
Latent classes enter the event process only through the generated random
effects or marker weights. There is no additional direct class coefficient
unless the analyst deliberately supplies an equivalent observed covariate in
the event formula.

Event times are drawn by inverse-transform sampling. Thus, when a clustered
block contributes to an association, event information can become informative
about posterior class membership during fitting.

# Correspondence with the fitted model

The generative simulator samples \(C_j\) and then samples \(Z_j\mid C_j\).
Stan cannot sample discrete parameters using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. During
fitting, `joinme_mix()` instead evaluates

\[
p(\boldsymbol{z}_j)
=
\sum_{g=1}^{G}
\pi_{jg}p_g(\boldsymbol{z}_j)
\]

with `log_sum_exp`. This is the exact marginal distribution induced by the
simulation procedure. The recorded simulated class is therefore useful for
validation but is not supplied to Stan.

# Quantities for recovery studies

The principal truth records are:

- `truth$mixture$probability`;
- `truth$mixture$probability_by_unit`;
- `truth$mixture$allocation`;
- `truth$mixture$location`;
- `truth$mixture$scale`;
- `truth$mixture$coefficient`;
- `truth$mixture$dimensions` and `starts`; and
- `truth$mixture$standardised_draws`.

Class recovery should be evaluated using posterior probabilities, proper
scoring rules and permutation-aware comparisons where ordering is absent.
Hard classification accuracy alone discards uncertainty and can appear
favourable in strongly imbalanced simulations.

# Limits of interpretation

A simulated class is a component label, not a diagnosis. Strongly separated
locations represent an intentionally favourable recovery problem. Scientific
simulation should also include overlapping scales, rare classes, misspecified
class counts, weak class-covariate effects, alternative shrinkage families and
event censoring. Conclusions about an estimator should be based on this wider
design rather than on a single conspicuous separation scenario.
